html:
The palace of the kings of France, about 20 km south-west of Paris, built up from a hunting lodge by Louis XIV from 1661. In 1682 he moved the court and the government there, and it stayed the seat of power until 1789.

The palace was a tool of rule. The great nobles had to live at court to win favour, under the king's eye and away from their own lands, and daily life was a ritual built around him. The Hall of Mirrors, 73 metres long, faced gardens laid out by André Le Nôtre with canals and hundreds of fountains. Courts across Europe copied it.

It also marks later turns:

  • in October 1789, in the French Revolution, a crowd of Paris women marched here and brought the royal family back to the city;
  • in 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors;
  • in 1919 the treaty that ended the First World War with Germany was signed in the same room.
